en: The Bouquet of Flowers of Reasoning (Nyāyakusumāñjali).
First Chapter:
Spreading through the wings of the virtuous, its festival bound to the awakening of the fragrance of the good, it does not wither under pressure; it is the essence of nectar.
A land where flowing honey-wine abounds.
May this faultless [work], which revolves like a bee upon the pair of feet of the Lord,
delight my mind without obstacle. (2)
A Handful of Flowers of Reasoning. //1//
The wise declare that meditation upon Him is the path to both heaven and liberation;
it is this Supreme Self who is described here. //2//

[1.102] Here, although those seeking any human goal— such as the followers of the Upaniṣads who say he is "pure and enlightened by nature," the followers of Kapila who say he is the "primordial knower" (ādividvān) and the perfected one (siddha), and those who say he is "untouched by afflictions, karma, its results, and latent impressions, and having presided over an emanation-body (nirmāṇakāya), he illuminates the tradition"— [...the text continues...]
The followers of Patañjali [hold that he] is the one who bestows grace;
the Mahāpāśupatas [hold that he is] independent and untainted even by actions contrary to worldly and Vedic norms.
The Śaivas call him Śiva; the Vaiṣṇavas, Puruṣottama; and the Paurāṇikas, Pitāmaha.
The ritualists call him the "Sacrificial Person" (yajñapuruṣa);
the Buddhists, "Everywhere" (sarvatra); the Digambaras, "Obstruction" (nivāraṇa).
The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that [the self] is taught as an object of worship,
while the Cārvākas hold that it is established by worldly convention. (5)
The Naiyāyikas maintain that he is endowed with whatever has been described;
what need is there for more? Even craftsmen worship him as Viśvakarman;

in him alone, his power is renowned throughout the cycle of existence (āsaṃsāram), just like [the renown of] caste, lineage, ancestral rite (pravara), Vedic school (caraṇa), family, and religious duties.
Since that state is the Blessed One, how could there even be doubt? What remains to be investigated?
Nevertheless—this investigation into logic regarding the Lord is designated as "reflection" (manana).
Meditation alone is performed, which follows immediately after hearing. //3//

For the Blessed One has been heard of many times in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas; now He must be reflected upon, according to the Vedic injunction: "He is to be heard and He is to be reflected upon. And as it is said: "By means of scripture, by inference, and by the relish of the practice of meditation..."
By conceptualizing wisdom in three ways, one attains the supreme yoga.
And because of this traditional teaching (smṛti):
"Therefore, here in brief, there are five types of misconception: [the first is] because of the non-existence of any supramundane means for achieving the next world;
[the second is] because it is possible to practice the means for achieving the next world in other ways [than those prescribed by scripture];..."
This is because there exists a means of valid cognition that reveals its non-existence; even if it were to exist, such a [means] would not be a valid cognition;
and because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition that establishes it.

[Ku. 1.105] Among these, the first alternative is not tenable; for: "Because of dependence, because of beginninglessness, because of diversity, because of universal activity, because of individual restriction, and because of experience, there exists a non-worldly cause. (4)
For this saṃsāra is not of manifold kinds.
That which consists of suffering ought to be independent;
for in that case, it would either certainly exist or certainly not exist, but it could never exist only occasionally.
If it is argued that it arises quite spontaneously, we say no: there is neither a negation of the existence of causes, nor a positive assertion of its own non-existence;
nor is this a description of its intrinsic nature, because such a state is restricted by a temporal limit. //5//
[aku.1.107] If the cause is negated, then because its existence would be independent, it would exist at all times, since there would be no distinction;
if existence itself is negated, [it would follow that it never exists].
Just as before, there is likewise no coming into being afterwards, because there is no difference [in the state of the entity].
Since that which is itself non-existent prior to its arising lacks the capacity for its own production, the position that it arises "from itself" is untenable.
Furthermore, the causal relationship is one of necessity.
Nor can it be both prior and posterior,
because reality cannot be the locus of differentiation;
for if that which is indefinable were the cause, the consequence would be its existence prior [to the effect], and from that, its status as eternal would follow.

It might be argued as follows: "We do not intend to assert a mere negation of a cause (*kāraṇaniṣedhamātra*), nor a negation of arising (*bhavanapratiṣedha*), nor self-causality (*svātmahetukatva*), nor causality by the indefinable (*nirupākhyahetukatva*).
Rather, we say that there exists some thing that is independent (*anapekṣa*) and possesses a nature determined by time, just like [things] possess a nature determined by place. (11) (12)
No, for if there were no limit or if the limit were indefinite, the quality of being occasional (*kādācitkatva*) would be contradicted.
For being occasional does not consist merely in being established at a later time; rather, it consists in existing only after having previously been non-existent.
But if it has a limit, that very same prior cause is said to be the limit.

If it is argued that the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) alone is the limit, we say no; for other things also exist at that time, otherwise the definition of that very non-existence would be impossible.
And thus, that [prior non-existence] cannot have a single limit, because there is no distinction;
for if prior non-existence were a limit independently of anything else, it would follow that the effect must exist even before that limit.

If it is argued that while there may be certain limits (*avadhi*), they are not required, and this is the meaning of "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*)— then what is the meaning of "they are not required"?
Does it mean that they are not fixed (*aniyata*)?
Or are they, even when restricted, incapable of being helpful?
In the first case, smoke— just like fire— would take even a donkey as its object,
because there would be no restrictive factor.
But in the second case, what is the need for another assistance?
For the very purpose of the restriction (niyama) is that which is required,
and it is precisely that [restriction] which constitutes the nature of the cause.
And since such a theory of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavāda) is accepted, this is like the restriction of an impermanent intrinsic nature.
For it is not appropriate to say, "If the reality of space is not accidental, why should it not be so for everything else? If you say this, we reply: no.
Because it is impossible for everything to possess an intrinsic nature;
for indeed, a single thing cannot have multiple intrinsic natures, as that would involve a contradiction.

[Objection: But surely, here too, it would always follow that there is a contradiction of its own nature as something occasional; thus the refutation is the same. [Reply: It is not the same. For if there were no limit, or if the limit were indefinite, the nature of being occasional would be contradicted; whereas if the limit is fixed, one must admit the doctrine of causality.
It might be argued: "The prior [moment] is the cause of the subsequent."
Let the northern [limit] be the boundary for the eastern [direction], and both [limits] be the boundary for the middle [direction];
for since perception is undeniable,
this must be accepted even by you.
For non-existence (abhāva), like existence (bhāva), does not possess two limits;
likewise, it would follow that even among existents where each extreme is unperceived, there would be no such thing—yet this is not so, because of beginninglessness.
This stream has no beginning, nor does it possess a single power belonging to a different genus.
One should be diligent regarding reality through the methods of positive and negative concomitance. //6//
[Ku. 1.114] For antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) has a limit in subsequent time and is beginningless; likewise, a positive entity (*bhāva*) such as a jar would also be so.

If it is argued that this is not undesirable because it concerns jars and the like whose prior limit is unperceived, we say no—if its very nature were limited to that much [duration], then just as on that day, on the previous day as well, having made that [prior limit] its boundary, there would be [the same state] for what follows it.
Because there would be no other state to depend upon;
likewise for each preceding stage as well. If it were to exist, then that very thing would be eternal.
If it is argued that its nature is such that it must exist on that very day, we say no; for by the same logic applied previously, it would follow that even that day existed previously.
Therefore, that [day] also must have been preceded by it, and likewise the one preceding that; thus, the doctrine of beginninglessness alone is superior.

But since there is no production of what was previously non-existent, it is impossible for any such unprecedented thing to come into being. Even so, if it is argued that the restriction should apply with respect to the individual (vyakti) and not with respect to the universal (jāti), we say: no.
Because it would contradict the nature of having a fixed genus. For if something, arising from whatever cause, were to possess that specific genus as its intrinsic nature,
then everything would either belong to every genus or belong to a single genus.
If its nature were such that it must arise from something of that same kind, then everything would have to be of every kind, or else of a single kind.
[Kv 1.116] How then is fire, arising from grass, a flint, or a gem, of a single kind? (16)
If it is argued that this is because they possess a single power, we say no;
for if a single capacity to produce an effect of the same kind were indeed inherent even in heterogeneous things, [then the distinction between them would vanish].
A specific cause could never be inferred from its effect;
nor could the exclusion of an effect belonging to that same class be determined by the exclusion of the cause,
because even in the absence of that [specific cause], it is possible for that effect to arise from something else that possesses the capacity for that same class.
If it is argued that the establishment [of categories] will proceed as far as perception extends, we say no;
for no causal basis (nimitta) is perceived, and what is actually perceived cannot serve as its own causal basis.
By this, the argument that [smoke arises] "because it belongs to the same genus as the subtle" (due to its being of one genus with the subtle) is refuted;
for then smoke would also have to arise from fire, since fire too possesses that subtlety.

If it is argued that the distinction or non-distinction of the genus of the effect depends solely on the distinction or non-distinction of the inherent cause (*samavāyin*), and not on the efficient or non-inherent causes (*nimitta* and *asamavāyin*), this is not so;
for it would follow that those two [types of causes] are not causes at all.
For it is not the case that existence [occurs] merely when [a cause] exists,
but rather that existence occurs only when [that cause] exists.
Furthermore, in the determination of a universal (jāti), the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) alone is not the basis.
Rather, it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Otherwise, if substance, quality, and action shared a single material cause (*ekopādānaka*), they would not be of different classes (*vijātīyatva*);
nor is it tenable to claim that this principle does not apply to a product-substance (*kāryadravya*).
Because we observe that curd is produced from very same constituent parts from which milk was previously begun;
by this, the restriction in the theory of apoha is refuted,
as it would lead to the undesirable consequence of the confusion of "this" (tyādi) and other such terms.

[The opponent claims: "By way of destruction, the restriction is based solely on the individual instance"—this is not so; for just as there is a restriction of modality such that [fire arises] from grass and the like only by means of blowing, from fire-sticks only by means of friction, and from a gem only by means of reflected sunbeams, so too there exists a distinction in the class of effects manifested by those very [causes].
And it is observed that, although there is no difference in their nature as fire, a lamp produces an illumination that pervades the interior of a palace;
whereas a wood-fire, though dense with a mass of flames, does not do so, and a cow-dung fire even less so.
But for one who does not perceive that [specificity], it would follow that he could infer the mere cause through the generality of the effect; what is there that is untenable?
If this were so, then even in the case of smoke and the like, there would have to be some unperceivable particularity.
For one who requires the perception of burning [as a probans], the establishment of the generality of fire does not follow from the generality of smoke and so forth;
by this, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is explained.

And if it is argued that, since the logical mark (*liṅga*) of the non-perception of an effect has thus been refuted, the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is also unestablished, and therefore inference is no longer applicable—[we reply: No.
This blow falls upon the head of the Buddhist who asserts that a difference in genus (*jātibheda*), which is within the scope of perception and non-perception, is not the determinant of the effect.

For us, however, the determination of the causal relation between two things occurs precisely in that manner when they possess positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) while being pervaded by a commonality;
and thus, even if there exists a further internal distinction, there is no contradiction for us.
[Ku. 1.121] But what, then, is the causal factor for the generality of fire (*dahanasāmānya*) in grass and other fuels?
If it is argued that this is because the specificities of the grass and so forth are restricted [to their respective effects], we say no.
Wind is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) for the production of mere light (*tejomātra*).
The conjunction of parts is the non-inherent cause;
the parts of light are the inherent causes.
This very same collection, when accompanied by a substance possessing gravity, constitutes the cause for a massed aggregate.
This very [fire] is burning in dependence upon the manifestation of touch belonging to the fire-element;
therein too, having reached water, it is divine,
and having reached earth, it is terrestrial.
That one undertakes the production of the internal [body] by obtaining both [causes] is to be inferred by oneself.

Nevertheless, let there be a single cause of a uniform nature; what is the use of a manifold [cause]? For it is observed that even that which is non-distinct [in its cause] can produce many distinct effects.

If it is argued that a single lamp is simultaneously the remover of darkness, the transformer of the wick, and the producer of the conventional usage of other forms [of light], we say no, because of the diversity of its effects.
There is never a sequence for a single entity, nor can there be diversity in what is unitary.
Furthermore, a difference in causal capacities cannot exist within an undifferentiated nature; such a nature is inviolable. (7)

[ku.1.123] First of all, multiple effects do not arise from a single cause that is independent [of other factors], because it is impossible for sequential effects to arise from what is non-sequential.
To begin with, regarding sequential effects...
If it is argued that because its nature is causal, it is thus [simultaneous], just like simultaneity itself—
(26) this too is a rebuttal regarding momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), but not regarding the theory of auxiliary causes (*sahakārivāda*).
If there were no dependence on each preceding factor, the very notion of sequence would be contradicted; however, if there is a fixed order of sequence, such independence is untenable.
Nor can it be manifold and yet devoid of variety.
(27) For if the cause of burning were neither deficient nor excessive [in its nature] as the cause of non-burning, then it would be neither non-burning nor burning; rather,
it would possess the nature of both.
Or it might be so; but it is not thus.

If it is argued that this is not a fault because of a difference in capacities (*śakti*), we say no—because that [capacity] is untenable given the difference or non-difference of the substrata (*dharmin*).
If it is argued that this is not a fault because its nature is to produce both [fire and smoke] without confusion, we say no;
for its non-burning nature is not under its own control,
but rather depends on the nature of that which produces it.
And likewise, since fire is dependent upon that [fuel], by whom can its reality be denied?
For when that [fire] is to be produced, it is not the case that this [fuel] does not possess that nature.
Therefore, because the effect is manifold, the cause must also be manifold.
And yet, it does not exist in that way by way of its own intrinsic nature;
therefore, there is an entry into a variety of auxiliary conditions.
However, even a single moment cannot come to be in such a manner independently of those [conditions].
[Objection: Let there be only the observed collection of auxiliary causes; what is the use of postulating an *apūrva* (unseen force)? [Response: No—for it is based on the activity of the world.
The activity of the world is neither fruitless, nor does it have suffering alone as its result.
Nor is there such a deception as this, which yields the fruit of visible gain. //8//
For if the mere succession of the transformations of preceding elements were the sole cause for each subsequent one,
then no one seeking the next world would engage in sacrifices (iṣṭa) or works of public utility (pūrta);
indeed, not even a single person acting with foresight would exert themselves in what is fruitless or has suffering as its only result.
How much more so, then, the world!
If you argue that it is for the sake of gain, honor, and fame—then what is the cause of gain and the rest?
For this activity is not, by its very nature, the cause of them.
Or rather, for what purpose is that which he is to obtain, or he who will honor him?
It is for the sake of fame and for the sake of affection.
If it is argued that "people are attached to one who gives and honors them,

for prosperity indeed arises from the affection of the people," this is not so; because the institution of giving and other such acts is established solely among ministers of policy and pleasure for that very purpose.
If it is argued that those who practice the austerity of the three Vedas are merely rogues in disguise, we say no; for they are of no use toward any visible prosperity.

If it is argued that they act in such a way for the sake of happiness, we say no; for then it would follow that even atheists would act in the same way, just as they do in the pursuit of sensual enjoyment.

If it is argued that even though [the result] is fruitless, it is nevertheless performed because it is established by worldly convention— just as the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) is performed because it is established by Vedic convention— this is the opinion of the Guru,
not the opinion of the Teacher (Guru).
Therefore, it is not appropriate to state this at such an improper time.
If you argue that this is because children are deceived by the elders, we say no; for the elders themselves also engage in such activity.
Furthermore, those who deceive others do not deceive even themselves.

If it is argued that those [earlier teachers] were likewise taught by their elders, and thus this tradition is beginningless— then in that case, there is no one here with the intent to deceive, from which a suspicion of fraud might arise.
If it is argued that some rogue, having first performed this for himself, subsequently causes others to perform it, then is he not truly someone who transcends the entire world?

How can one regard as a single person that individual who, for the sake of mere curiosity to deceive others, throughout his entire life exhausts himself through celibacy, austerity, and faith— giving away all his possessions as sacrificial fees, abandoning all kinsmen, and turning his back on all pleasure?
How indeed can one look upon him as such?
Would even those who act first follow him?
Or by what mark has he been determined by you, possessed of such supramundane wisdom, to be a deceiver?
For the pleasure of deceiving is not weightier than this mass of suffering.
(31) If it is argued that this is seen even among those considered heretics, we say no—because there is a distinction based on the presence or absence of a discernible cause.

Furthermore, if such a practice were extended over an beginningless time, deception would occur merely through the instruction of great expenditure of wealth and effort by resorting to another method;
but not through an action that lies outside the scope of actual performance. (32) [Therefore, the latter is not a case of deception.]
Otherwise, even the well-known status of being a heretic (*pākhaṇḍitva*) would not exist without contradicting valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that the very diversity of giving, study, and so forth constitutes the cause for the diversity of the world, we say no— because of their momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*),
and because that which is required [as a cause] must occur at a later time.

An action that has long since perished is not capable of producing a fruit without a residual potency (*atiśaya*); nor can there be enjoyment [of the fruit] by those who are indistinguishable [from one another], even if they were conditioned by the primary elements (*bhūta*). (33)9.
Therefore, there must be some excellence [in them].

If it is argued that these very things, having arisen through the power of their own causes, are the means for the attainment of restricted enjoyment— then is this an imperceptible form of theirs, or a distinction among their auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*)?
First of all, that which is perceptible by the senses cannot have a supersensible nature, because that would involve a contradiction.
In the second case, however, there is the establishment of the *apūrva* (the unseen force).
Let it be established as a property of the elements itself, though supersensible, just like gravity (*gurutva*) and other such qualities.
You must also necessarily accept this;
otherwise, how could there be an obstruction by means of mantras and the like?
For instance, it is observed that fire burns only when it comes into contact with the palm of the hand in a certain manner.
When there is an obstruction by means of such mantras and the like, burning does not occur; but when it is absent, it does occur.
In that case, we do not perceive any deficiency in the visible causes.
Nor can an unseen deficiency be presumed when a seen excellence is present,
because that [seen excellence] serves precisely this purpose.
Otherwise, even in the case of ritual action, a distinction [between success and failure] might never arise.
Nor is the causal complex qualified by the absence of an obstructer the cause; for an absence is not a cause,
as it is a mere nothingness (*tuccha*).
Furthermore, because the effect arises even without that [obstructing factor] at the time when the application of the obstructer and the promoter occurs;
and because, through the dilemma of whether it exists prior to or after [the effect], there would follow the consequence of having an indefinite cause;
and because that which is incapable of acting cannot logically function as an obstructer.
Furthermore, since it is accepted that there is some causal efficacy (*kiñcitkaratva*) in the case of supersensible power (*atīndriya-śakti*),
and because an effect does not arise even when the mutual absence (*itaretarābhāva*) [of obstacles] is present during the employment of mantras and the like,
therefore some supersensible factor conducive to burning is inferred as an auxiliary (*anugrāhaka*) of fire.
That whose presence as an obstacle is logically established when others are performing harm; that in the absence of which the effect arises;
and that by virtue of whose uniformity the contingency of having an indefinite cause is discarded.
To this it is replied: Just as an existent thing (*bhāva*) is considered a cause in its own nature, so too is a non-existent thing (*abhāva*) considered a cause like an effect.
Obstruction (*pratibandha*) is the lack of causal completeness (*visāmagrī*); that which causes it is the obstructor (*pratibandhaka*). //10//
For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the fact that non-existence (*abhāva*) is not a cause;
for it is not the case that because this [non-existence] is void in its positive form (*vidhirūpa*), it is likewise so in its own nature (*svarūpa*);
otherwise, even a positive entity would be [void].
Because it would follow that [the cause] is a mere nothingness;
for if it is argued that since causality is pervaded by existence, causality ceases upon the cessation of that [existence], we say no— because that would lead to a circularity.

Furthermore, since the conformity to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-anuvidhāna*), which is the ground for determining causality, is equally present in the case of absence as it is in the case of existence;
if it is argued that "the presence of absence is unavoidable, but not by way of being a cause," this is the same [for both].
If it is argued that "its presence is prompted by something else because it displaces its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)," this is likewise the same.
If it is argued that the exclusion of non-existence is the very nature of existence, then the exclusion of existence by non-existence likewise does not differ from its own nature.
Therefore, just as the restriction that "only the existence of an entity is the producer" is untenable, so too is the restriction that "only an existent entity is the producer."
For what indeed is the distinction between these two?
However, there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) at the time of applying the obstructer (pratibandhaka) and the stimulator (uttambhaka);
that is, if the non-arising of the effect occurs when such conditions are present.
Only if that were the case would there be arising;
but it is not so, because even then the counteragent is absent. For [an entity] whose counteragent is non-existent—(35)
The mantra considered to be an obstacle is the counteragent;
however, such a thing does not exist at all.
That which does exist is not a counteragent.

If it is argued that even so, there is merely an absence of the qualifier while the qualified object remains present— and since that [absence] occurs only when the inciting mantra is present, the causal complex is entirely different— [we reply: no,
because the qualified entity itself is likewise absent.
For it is not logical that when there is one who possesses a staff, others who do not possess staves are thereby non-existent; rather, it is only the absence of the staff itself [that is absent].
Just as when there is the mere presence of a staff, [others may still exist].
Whether both exist or both are absent, the absence of the solitary Puruṣa is everywhere the same;
likewise when there is the presence of the solitary sustainer (uttambhaka).
It should be understood that whether there is the presence of both the obstructer and the counter-obstructer, or the absence of both, the mere absence of the obstructer remains the same.
Now, why is this triad of causal conditions not accepted as such?
Because the effect does not deviate from that [cause];
because there is no means of valid cognition for postulating a distinction between types of universals;
and because it is established by what has already been stated.
Or, if it exists, let it be so; what loss is there for us?
Furthermore, the alternative of prior destruction (*prākpradhvaṃsa*) does not entail the consequence of having an indefinite cause, since that [destruction] being present, the effect is not produced.
"In its absence alone it arises"— here, it is precisely the relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*) that serves as the causal factor.
As for one who, failing to discern the distinction between relational non-existence and the negation of identity (*tādātmya*), objects on the basis of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*):
That [objection] should be answered as follows:
even so, since there is no "universal" (jāti) in non-existent things, how could there be a grasping of the three?
And if they are not grasped, how can their status as causes be determined? If this is asked—let there be no universal.

For it is not the case that only those things grasped by that [cause] serve as factors in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of all transactions involving limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

By this [argument], it follows that even when an obstructing factor exists, because another thing of the same kind might be absent, there would be the undesirable consequence of the production of the effect.

The claim that even in the case of non-arising there is something further to be depended upon has been refuted. For it is established that "when that which belongs to a certain class exists, the effect arises; by implication, when it does not exist, it does not arise. Thus, even if that [specific cause] is present, the effect ought not to occur if another instance of that same class is absent. (36)
This is not so;
for even when there is an unfavorable condition, since there is an absence of other instances of that same class, it is incapable of producing any effect.
As for the claim that "it is incapable of producing any effect," that too is incorrect.

The primary object of obstruction is the deficiency of the causal complex (*sāmagrīvaikalya*); and in this context, that [deficiency] is precisely the mantra and so forth. However, these [mantras, etc.
are not themselves the obstructing agent.
What follows from that, given its inefficacy?
Its instigators, however, are the obstructors, and since they are indeed efficacious, what is inconsistent about this?
But those who explain that "the non-arising of the effect itself is the obstruction" have effectively stated that "obstructors are obstructors even without performing an obstruction."

For instance, the non-arising of an effect would have to be either its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or its attainment of another time. It cannot be the former, because that [prior non-existence] is not something to be produced.
Not the second, because time is non-different in its essential nature;
and as for its limiting adjuncts, they depend upon their own causes even without a mantra.
If it is argued that the temporal adjunct which delimits prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is dependent upon that [non-existence], we say no—because that [adjunct] exists even before the mantra.

Therefore, since there is a rule of priority and posteriority between the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and its effect, a temporal sequence is figuratively attributed to their absences as well; in reality, however, they are simultaneous, so this path [of argumentation] is not tenable.

[Ku. 1.136] If this is not so, then even if one accepts the existence of a capacity (*śakti*), what is the remedy? For instance, is the capacity destroyed by the obstructing factor, or is it its property (*dharma*) that is destroyed?
The positions are as follows: either another property is produced, or nothing at all is produced.
In that regard, since it is impossible for something that performs no function to act as an obstacle, [the obstacle must] produce a contrary property.
The acceptance of non-existence as a cause implies that the effect occurs only when that [non-existence] is present,
which opens the door to the conceptual alternatives of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth;

furthermore, if that [non-existence] is destroyed, or if its property is destroyed, and it is then produced again by an excitant (*uttambhaka*), there would be the fault of having an indefinite cause (*aniyatahetukatva*).
Previously [the production was] from that which produces its own nature (*svarūpa*); now it is from the stimulator (*uttambhaka*).

Nor is it correct to argue that this is not so because they belong to the same class due to having identical powers (*samānaśaktikatā*); for the existence of identical power among things of different classes (*vijātīya*) is denied.

Nor is it tenable to claim that the stimulator merely destroys the obstructing power and does not produce the positive capacity [of the effect]; for that would entail the consequence that such a capacity is never produced.
If that [effect] arises from a specific time, then that very thing is what is called "having an indeterminate cause.
It might be argued: "Let there be no innate power (sahaja-śakti);
however, there may be an acquired power (ādheya-śakti)."
For the refinement (*abhisaṃskāra*) of rice and other grains is indeed observed through sprinkling and other such rites;
otherwise, how could those very same grains be employed for specific effects at a later time?

Nor is it tenable to say that they produce the effect only upon obtaining the mantras and so forth as auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), because the effect arises even when those [mantras] have long since perished.
Nor are they [the sacrifices] accompanied by their own destruction;
for if that were so, the very destructions of the sacrifices and other acts would produce heaven and the like, rendering the postulation of an *apūrva* (unseen potency) unnecessary.

If it is argued that because those [acts] are infinite, an infinite flow of results would follow— then even if the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is postulated, why would the flow of results not be exactly as great?
If it is argued that this is due to the very nature of the *apūrva*, then the same applies here as well.
Even by that much, the destruction of that [object] does not perish; this is the distinction.
It might be argued: "Sprinkling and so forth are *upalakṣaṇas* (indicators), but not *viśeṣaṇas* (qualifiers)."
And if it is argued that rice and other grains, though characterized by those [names] which do not actually exist, will be employed here and there—
just as a commentary is [characterized] by its author (guru) or a field by its cultivator (kuru)— that is incorrect.
For no one maintains that a secondary characteristic (upalakṣaṇa) possesses causality even in the absence of its own essential nature (svarūpa) and activity (vyāpāra),
as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Rather, it is merely conventional usage (vyavahāra) that is accomplished by the cognition of that [characteristic].
But that [result] is not produced by it;
even that knowledge is dependent upon its own causes,
and it is not produced by that [cause] which has perished without leaving a trace (*niranvaya*).
(Granted for now) Or let there be the postulation of a further excellence even in that case;
what is lost or severed?
Alternatively, let it be that [the word] also serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for sacrifice and so forth.
The time characterized by that [action], or the sacrificer himself, will accomplish heaven and so forth; what is the use of an *apūrva*?

Furthermore, Devadatta’s body and other things are not drawn toward him by his own qualities for the sake of experience, because they are the means for his experience, just like a garland and the like—[this is the inference].
It is not correct to say that there is no lack of distinction because the *apūrva* is established through positive concomitance (*anvaya*);
for [the argument] would result in proving what is already established by means of desire, effort, and cognition as appropriate.
Nor is it logical that experience occurs even for those devoid of those [mental states].

The meaning to be proven is not that [the cognition] is produced by its own qualities, because [if it were so], there would be inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) due to the mind (*manas*). Furthermore, [the cognition] would be established as even superior to that [previous cognition].
Nor is it produced by its own qualities; this is the point to be proven, since [otherwise] there would be inconclusiveness with respect to the mind.

Nor is the reason qualified by the condition "being an effect"; for even so, the proof would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of those very secondary characteristics (*upalakṣaṇa*).
If it is asked, "How can things that are non-existent be producers?", this [objection] applies equally to consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) and the like as well.
Therefore, it is only by producing a positive excellence (*atiśaya*) that sprinkling and other such rites are capable of bringing about a result occurring at a later time;
for they are undertaken for that purpose on the basis of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like sacrifice, agriculture, and medical treatment.
Otherwise, it would follow that agriculture and the like would be impossible to accomplish.

Because seeds and the like undergo destruction down to their ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), and because there is no intermediate genus (*avāntarajāti*) within them, it would be impossible for them to initiate an effect of a determinate genus.
To this, it is replied: [Verse 1.141] It is held that the impression (*saṃskāra*) belongs to the person alone [and is produced] by sprinkling, washing, and so forth;
whereas the specific qualities of the atoms, such as those born of heating (*pākaja*), are their own inherent attributes (*svaguṇa*). //11//
For just as oblations of clarified butter, offered with mantras into the fire for the sake of a particular deity, consecrate the person [who offers them],
and not the fire, nor the deities;
Similarly, sprinkling and other such rites performed with reference to rice and the like sanctify only the person, not the rice itself.

And thus, through the connection of the person who is the substratum of the impression produced by the *kārīrī* sacrifice, there occurs in the clouds the action consisting of movement and the shedding of water;
likewise, there occur in the rice and other materials their respective subsequent specific actions.
And just as in one case there is an absence of fruit due to defects in the agent, the object, or the means, so it is in the other case as well;
for the status of being based on scripture (*āgamikatva*) is equal in both instances.
In that case, there could not be a further subsequent use for rice and the like, just as there is none for the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

Or, if it were for the sake of utility, another thing of the same kind might also be employed, since there would be no distinction [between them]. This is not so, for volitional formations (*abhisaṃskāra*) are diverse.
Some are effective in producing an effect only when they are active, possess a specific objective, and have auxiliary factors.
What can be done in this matter?
For destiny is difficult to overcome.

Just as the ritual effect of a malevolent rite (*abhicāra-saṃskāra*), when performed with reference to a particular body, produces suffering only for that specific person connected to it and not for anyone else; so too is it here.
Nor is it independent of them;
likewise, even though consecrations (*saṃskāra*) such as *abhimantraṇa* (invocation with mantras) do exist, they are not of the slightest use [if the substance were independent].

If it is asked, "In that case, how is it that rice and other grains function as the object of the action to be consecrated (*saṃskārya-karman*)?", [the answer is: precisely because of their connection with the fruit of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other such rites.

[Ku. 1.143] Now, if it is argued that there is an inference to the effect that whatever is performed with a specific object in view must produce some effect upon that object—just as the *putreṣṭi* and *pitṛyajña* sacrifices do for their respective objects—and likewise, consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) and other rites are undertaken with rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth in view; we say: no, because this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of the offering of oblations (*havis-tyāga*) and similar acts.
For they do not produce anything in the fire or other [objects] that is conducive to a fruit arising at a later time.

Or rather, is it not observed that the operations of the sense-faculties, logical marks, and words— engaged with respect to an object of cognition— produce something only in the cognizer, and not in the object of cognition?

If it is argued that agriculture and medicine should also be understood in this same way, we say no; for since the transformation of things—such as the color produced by baking (*pākaja-rūpa*)—is accounted for by visible causes alone, there is no evidence for postulating an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
This is likewise the case with the application of lac-dye and similar treatments.
These have been explained.
For this very reason, even when a particular seed is destroyed down to its ultimate atoms (paramāṇu),
and even though those atoms lack any intermediate generic class (jāti), [the continuity of the species persists].
Atoms, distinguished precisely by specific qualities produced by prior cooking, initiate their respective particular effects;
for instance, a rice seed [is distinct] from barley and so forth.
Just as the seed of a human or a monkey is distinguished from that of a cow or a buffalo by its genus (*jāti*),
so too do those atoms which constitute the fundamental basis become distinguished solely by their being produced through heating (*pākaja*).
For it is impossible that cow’s milk should be fragrant, sweet, and cold,
while its atoms are the opposite;
therefore, the atoms must indeed be produced by such [specific] heating.

Whether it be the excellence of the first moment or the excellence of the final moment, or even the sprout and so forth, they exist exactly as they are; what need is there here for the postulation of a "potency" (*śakti*)?
It is exactly the same at the beginning of a kalpa as well.
Now, the bringing together of seeds and so forth by people such as ourselves is [the case];
however, at that time, the mutual conjunction of already separated things occurs solely from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). This is the distinction.
Nor should it be argued that why should it not be the same even now;

for if agricultural and other such activities were abolished, there would follow the abolition of the enjoyments produced by them, and because of the fear of disorder, [the existence of] unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) [is required].
(45) [Karmas]
It is inferred that the means of enjoyment are established solely through the arrangement of perceived actions.
Therefore, atoms, distinguished by specific qualities produced by cooking (*pākaja*) and by specific configurations (*saṃsthāna*), initiate specific effects;
and these [qualities] arise from specific conjunctions with fire, air, and water.
And those [motions] arise from action;
and that [action] arises, as the case may be, from impulsion, impact, gravity, velocity, fluidity, and conjunction with the self possessed of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa). Thus, nothing is untenable.
And there are various distinctions among the efficient causes (nimitta).
Upon digestion, they become as follows:
for example, the flesh of a *hārīta* bird, when sprinkled with turmeric water and scorched by a turmeric fire, kills instantly upon consumption.
“Ghee kept for ten nights in a bronze vessel even turns into poison;
milk kept overnight in a copper vessel also becomes bitter,” and so forth.
In those cases, however, where there is no quality produced by cooking (*pākaja*) in water, fire, or air, [how is this explained]?
In that regard, how can there be specific qualities such as arising, non-arising, fluidity, or solidity?

Or alternatively, since there is no difference [in the nature of the object] even when a clay image or similar object is consecrated through rites such as *pratiṣṭhā*, why would merit arise from worship and so forth, while demerit arises from transgression; whereas in the case of an unconsecrated object, nothing at all [occurs]?

Nor should one perform assistance for another by means of the duty belonging to the sacrificer; for the duty of one person is not applicable to another, and if it were applicable, it would follow that it must be common to all.
To this, it is replied: "Arising, non-arising, and so forth, result from the conjunction with different causes."
Or else, it is [established] through recognition by means of the presence of the deity. //12//

[Ku. 1.148] For atoms, assisted by a specific unseen force (adṛṣṭa-viśeṣa) that brings them together, initiate a particular substance. From their specific nature, distinctions between manifest and unmanifest qualities arise.

In the same way, water, though its nature is fluidity, produces solid things such as hailstones when its fluidity is constrained by various specific conditions (*nimitta*); this and other points should be inferred by oneself.

Furthermore, images and the like attain the status of being objects of worship in their respective places because the specific presiding deities—such as Rudra, Upendra, and Mahendra—are brought into proximity through various ritual procedures, just as a king’s body, which has fainted from being bitten by a snake, is restored to consciousness by means of a procedure for removing poison.
And our view is that the presence of the notions of "I" (ahaṅkāra) and "mine" (mamakāra) therein belongs to those [who perceive it],
just as a king who sees his own likeness in a painting [identifies with it]. However,
for others, such a state should be understood to apply to an object of recognition that has been worshipped by successive generations, or to an object of established recognition.
By this, the consecrated water, sprouts, and so forth are explained.

[Objection: What then is the status regarding jars and the like? If you say it is "skillful" (i.e., they are effective), we say no; for that [consecration] does not dismantle the observed causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Nor is it unperceived,
because it is a means of cognition;
nor does it produce what is unperceived.

Because if [the cause] were always present for the production of the effect (dharma), victory would necessarily follow forever; and if it were otherwise, defeat would necessarily follow forever. To this, it is said: "The methods of investigation are intended for the examination of that which is already present [in the cause], solely for the sake of obtaining the manifestation (vṛttilābha) of the conditions for victory or its opposite. (1.150)

Although it is our established doctrine that "the presence of the presiding deities of Dharma and so forth is also brought about here, and they manifest a physical form corresponding to the power of their karma," nevertheless, we speak otherwise due to the contrary views of others.
For by that method as well, that very same cause of victory or defeat is manifested. (49)
It brings forth the effect that manifests it;
and the manifestation of the *karma* is precisely the acquisition of its auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*). And that auxiliary condition is: "I have mounted the scales according to this procedure."
It is the recognition that "I, who was an evildoer, am now indeed sinless.
As they say: "But the gods see them, as does one's own inner person (antarapuruṣa).
Alternatively, by depending on a purification consistent with his vow, dharma is produced by him.
It is unrighteous because it is prescribed as having a specific objective, because the fruit of victory is proclaimed, and because it depends upon impurity;
for it is prohibited by its result, since it demonstrates a fruit that is undesired, characterized by defeat. (50)
[Ku. 1.151] Now, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the negation of power (*śakti*)? None at all.
Does it, then, truly exist? Certainly.
For in our system, it is not the case that the category of power simply does not exist.
What, then, is that?
It is causality.
What is that? It is the state of having a nature determined by a prior time.
Or [it is] the state of possessing an absence of the effect due to the deficiency of auxiliary causes.
What then is the status regarding the negation of anything further than that? None at all.
Is it then merely an affirmation? That too—(51)
It does not exist, because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But then how can doubt arise in this way?
Because it has never been perceived before.
(52) If that is so, then where is the dispute?

Since the term "capacity" (*śakti*) is also applied to auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) because they share the common quality of being benefactors, [the dispute concerns] the distinction among those auxiliaries.
Even in that case—there certainly exists a further benefactor for fire and the like.
If you mean that [the object] is removed by obstructing factors, then we do not dispute this;

for even the Mīmāṃsakas, who lack [valid] means of knowledge, ought not to disagree once they admit that non-existence (*abhāva*) and the like serve as auxiliary factors (*anugrāhaka*) for our intended position.
Then— some maintain that non-existence and so forth are supportive factors,
while others say they are not;
thus, at the height of this dispute, the fact that these are supportive factors has been established.
What else remains for which a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be stated? Enough with this excessive detail.
Nevertheless, it is precisely this conscious entity that is being refined.
If it is asked, "How is it determined that [the body] is not composed of the elements (bhūta)?"—it is said in reply:

Since the enjoyers are eternal and all-pervading, they would reach all bodies without distinction; and because there would be no regulating factor even by means of specific elements, the fixed assignment of particular portions [of the body] could not be established.
For there is no rule that "this body, this mind, and these senses, though specific, belong to this [enjoyer] alone."
Because there is no restrictive factor (or because there is no distinction),
it would follow that [the self] possesses a common physical form;
yet this is not the case, for [the self] is not merely a property of the primary elements.
If it is argued that [the property] is uncommon (asādhāraṇa) with respect to some conscious being because its opposite is observed—
just as in the case of "duality" and so on— we say no; for that too, being equivalent to the body and other such things, falls within the scope of the subject (pakṣa).
Its restriction occurs precisely through the inclusion of the quality of determinate volition (*niyata-cetana*),
and not merely by virtue of being produced by it; for [the mere fact of being produced] is itself non-distinctive.

[Ku. 1.153] Even so, if it is asked: "Since the restriction is established simply by the fact of being produced from that, what is the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position (*vipakṣa*)?"—the consequence would be the collapse of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*);
for it is observed that the body and other such things produce those qualities only by taking up the attributes of a conscious being (*cetana*).
For example: effort (*prayatna*) arises by taking up desire (*icchā*).
Desire and the like are governed by knowledge, and pleasure and the like are governed by that [desire], and so forth.
If it is argued that even in the present case, it is only the intellect (*buddhi*) and other factors residing in the conscious being (*cetana*) that serve as the regulators, we say no; for...
Because those [elements] do not exist prior to the body and so forth;
and thus, since the conscious beings are without distinction and the elements are common [to all], a restriction regarding experience is not tenable.
By this, the Sāṅkhya doctrine is refuted;
for it is as follows:
the *puruṣa* is without cause, without effect, and is of the nature of immutable consciousness.

The primordial cause is *prakṛti*, which is insentient and subject to transformation; from it arises the creation beginning with the *mahat*. For consciousness (*cit*) itself does not possess the nature of being bound to objects.
Because it would follow that there is no liberation;
nor is primordial nature itself its own inherent nature,
for even so, because of its permanence, it would follow that there is no liberation.
Nor is the jar or the like itself directly its [object], because it is impossible for it to be both seen and unseen;
nor is it [the object] by way of the sense organ alone.
Because of the impossibility of distraction [from the object];
nor does it occur through the doors of the senses or the mind;
for even in the state of dreaming, a man who identifies himself as a boar, a tiger, or the like, still possesses the sense of self as a man.
Nor [is it established] by means of an activity extending up to the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*),
because even when that activity ceases during the state of deep sleep, the continuum of the effort for respiration persists.
Thus, that which persists as a single entity with activity throughout these various states,
and upon which the impressions of experience depend—
that is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). An object mounted upon it becomes a limiting adjunct (*upadhāna*) for the Puruṣa.

Furthermore, because one does not perceive their difference, there arises in that inactive Puruṣa the conceit of agency; and although he is insentient, there arises the conceit of sentience, and therein alone do actions find their culmination.
But the Puruṣa is like the leaf of a lotus. (55)
In every respect, it is untainted.
Perception is the function of the sense organs;
conceptualization, however, belongs to the mind.
Self-conceit belongs to the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); the determination of what is to be done belongs to the intellect (buddhi). For that intellect possesses three aspects.
The constituents [of this process] are the coloring by the person (puruṣoparāga), the coloring by the object (viṣayoparāga), and the entry of activity (vyāpārāveśa).
For there arises the thought, "This must be done by me.
In that context, the coloring by consciousness expressed as "by me" is unreal, like the reflection of a face on a mirror, due to the non-apprehension of their difference.
The coloring by an object as "this" is a transformation occurring through the channel of the senses, like the soiling of a mirror struck by breath; it is not ultimately real.
The functional activity also depends upon both of these.
In this context, knowledge is characterized by the coloring by an object, belonging to the intellect (buddhi) whose characteristic is such functional activity.
The connection with that [intellect], which is a non-real (atāttvika) superimposition upon the person— just as the dirtiness [of a face] appears in a face reflected in a mirror—
is what is called "apprehension" (upalabdhi).
Thus, all eight categories, beginning with dharma, belong to the intellect alone.
This is because [the object] is determined through its grammatical coreferentiality with that [intellect].

Nor is it logical to claim that the intellect itself is conscious by nature, because it is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*); the Puruṣa, however, is changeless and eternal (*kūṭasthānityatva*).
[Ku. 1.156] This too has already been refuted.
For it is said: "The controllers are the attributes of the agent, and he alone is the cognizer for us;
otherwise, there would be either no liberation or an eternal lack of transmigratory existence. (14)

It is established that properties such as dharma and so forth, which are situated in the same locus as volitional effort (*kṛti*), are the determinants [of agency]. Furthermore, the conscious being is indeed the agent;
for volitional effort and consciousness are experienced as being in a relation of co-locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Nor is this an error, because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*). If it is argued that "being directed by another" is the subverting evidence— just as in the case of a pot— that is not so, for that [reason] applies equally even to the status of being an agent.
And likewise, the activity of a Great Being would also not be natural.

If it is argued that this is not a fault because [the cause] is observed [to produce the effect], then the same applies [to our position]. If it is argued that "being produced by a non-conscious entity" is a subverting argument (bādhaka) because of the identity (tādātmya) between cause and effect, we say no— because that [identity] is unestablished (asiddhi).
For there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the fact that the creator himself is an effect;
on the contrary, by the principle stated in Nyāya-sūtra 3.1.25, "Because the birth of one free from passion is not observed," it is established that [the series] is indeed beginningless.

Furthermore, whatever form is observed in an effect must, if it is of the nature of its cause, imply that passion and the like would also have to be admitted as being within the *prakṛti*; and in that case, that [passion] itself would be the intellect (*buddhi*),
not the *prakṛti*.
If it is argued that because they are endowed with the eight qualities,
those [elements] exist there in a subtle form, having abandoned their grossness, then consciousness will likewise exist in that same way.
Nevertheless, the reason (hetu) remains unestablished.

If that were the case, it would follow that even jars and the like possess consciousness, because they are identical [to the self]. If this is argued, then the consequence that they must also possess passion and so forth is likewise unavoidable.
And subtlety is the same.
Therefore, whatever kind of effect is observed to arise from whatever kind of cause, one should infer that from a cause of such a nature, there arises only an effect of such a nature.
But it is not the case that the effect possesses as many properties as the cause, because of the possibility of deviation; so what is the point of this irrelevant matter?
And if cognition were eternal;
There would follow the consequence of no liberation,
because as long as the person always possesses adjuncts (*upādhi*), it does not abide in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Now, [if it is argued that] it dissolves...
Therefore, if there were a beginning characterized by the dissolution of various things and so forth,
who would be the controller during the state prior to their production?
For Prakṛti is common to all.
And thus there would be no cycle of saṃsāra.

If it is argued that, although [the cause] is common due to the persistence of the impressions (*vāsanā*) of each preceding cognition, it is nevertheless uncommon [to each individual], then it is shown that even when cognition ceases, the impression of its attributes persists.
If it is argued that there is no fault because of its subtlety (*saukṣmya*), then there would be the undesirable consequence of renewed activity even in liberation (*mukti*).
If it is argued that this is not so because [the intellect] lacks darkness (*tamas*), then let the intellect itself— possessing its own capacity and having a dormant nature— be *prakṛti*;
what is the use of postulating separate referents for the intermediate terms *prakṛti*, *ahaṃkāra*, and *manas*?

For that very [consciousness], through its association with various functions, is designated by this or that word—just like the bodily wind—and thus scripture also remains consistent; for this reason as well, the probans is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Liberation (*apavarga*) is the non-occurrence of consciousness due to the cessation of its domain.
The connection with latent impressions (vāsanā) constitutes the capacity for agency;
from that arises saṃsāra.
Furthermore, if there were an absolute difference between the attribute (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin), it would contradict the doctrine of immutability (kauṭasthya).
Furthermore, difference—characterized by the superimposition of contradictory properties—is established by perception, as in the case of a jar and a cloth.
Nor is there non-difference [of the two] on account of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);
for that consists in being denotable by the same word.
The state of being the object of a single cognition, the state of having a common substratum, and the relationship of locus and located.
Whether it be the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) or mere relation, these are possible only when there is difference; even in the case of difference,
they do not touch upon non-difference— thus all is clear.
[1.159] This might be so:
all this would indeed be the case if there were an eternal, omnipresent enjoyer.
But from what source does he exist?
Because only the primary elements (bhūta) possess sentience,
[they are] transformed into the form of a body.
If it is argued that those [causes] are indeed so, because they are perceived as such through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*),

and that the latencies (*vāsanā*) of karma and knowledge will persist everywhere, determined by each individual, thereby accounting for the necessity of experience and rebirth— then it is said in reply:
One person does not remember what was seen by another, nor does a single entity persist through the transition of births;
there is no transfer of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and for a stable [self], there is no other mode of movement. (15)
For consciousness does not reside solely in the aggregate of the elements;
for if it were different every day, there would follow the consequence that one could not remember what was experienced on preceding days. Nor does it reside solely in each [element] individually.
Because it is impossible to remember what was experienced by [the self] once the limbs such as the hands and feet have perished;
nor does a latent impression (vāsanā) transfer from one thing to another through contact, as in the case of musk scent on a garment.
Because it would follow that the embryo dwelling in the womb could remember what was experienced by the mother;
nor is the restriction of the relationship between material cause and its effect a valid solution, since such a relationship is absent in the case of atoms under the doctrine of permanence.
Furthermore, because disconnected parts cannot serve as the material cause for a composite whole that has been broken,
and because the previously established composite whole has perished,
let it be then that there is momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
Nor is the excellence (atiśaya) something distinct; rather, because it is obscured by similarity, it is not conceptualized immediately.
It is determined through the observation of effects that there is a final excellence;
and thus the primary elements themselves arise in such and such a manner that even the rules governing the reconnection of rebirth and so forth become logically possible.
This would be so if momentariness were established;
however, that very point has been refuted at length elsewhere.
Furthermore: "Without a difference in kind (vaijātya), that [causal relation] could not exist; and without it, there could be no inference."
Without that [ascertainment], there is no establishment of it; nor is there perception without ascertainment. (16)

For it is not the case that the establishment of momentariness follows from the admission that "in the cases of acting and not acting, the acquisition or non-acquisition of auxiliary causes is the determining factor for that which already exists as belonging to that same class";
because this is not contradictory even in the case of a single individual entity,
according to the principle that "there is no distinction between 'that' and 'such-and-such'."

Therefore, disregarding that heterogeneity (*vaijātya*) which is indeed unauthoritative (*aprāmāṇika*), one must accept it as such. And thus, due to the suspicion that "just as there is heterogeneity in the cause, so too might there be some heterogeneity in the effect for which there is a dependence on a cause, but not for that which belongs to a perceived genus," the establishment of its production [from that cause] is not achieved.

If it is argued that what is observed to be of a certain kind must be accidental, we say no— for even in that case, there will be some other distinct factor acting as the cause, which is not contradictory. If it is further argued that "no specific feature of the effect is perceived as being prompted by that [cause],
nor is any other prompter of the general class of effects observed," then is it not the case that a specific feature inherent in the cause itself is perceived as being the prompter for that [effect]?
Or, no other distinct purpose for the commonality of the cause is observed,
by which the intended proof might be established;
for doubt is easily incurred in both cases alike.

If it is argued that [the existence of the cause] is inferred from the production or non-production of the effect, we say no; for this is already accounted for by the mere presence or absence of auxiliary conditions. Or, even if it were so inferred, doubt would still arise regarding the effects.
Because there is no negator [of it].
For the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is not capable of negating that specific quality of smoke which is produced by fire;
for since that [quality] is determinable solely through its effect, its non-determination follows precisely from the non-perception of that effect.
Furthermore, because an effect may be beyond the reach of the senses,
for this very reason, even another type of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) finds no scope.
Thus, when two universals (*jāti*) exist in a state of opposition— whether they are positive in form or negative in form— there can be no coexistence.
Furthermore, there is a rule regarding the relationship of priority and posteriority between two co-inherent [universals];
for there is no evidence for postulating two universals that subsist neither less nor more extensively [than one another].
Since there is no difference in what is excluded, contradiction has no scope, and thus difference is untenable.
Furthermore, if there were a coexistence of two things that are mutually exclusive, it would follow that "cowness" and "horseness" could likewise exist together.
If you argue that this is not the case because of a contradiction between their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), we ask:
why is this so? If you say it is because they are always established through mutual exclusion, this too is not a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If it is argued that the coexistence of the causal complexes is inferred from the coexistence of their respective parts—

up to the point where it is said that this is because the two effects are by nature mutually exclusive— then in that case, there would be no coexistence of trembling and being a *śiṃśapā* tree, as these two are mutually exclusive. If you say, "But this [coexistence] is indeed observed," then what hope is there that the coexistence of "cowness" and "horseness" would not also be observed?
And thus, it has also been refuted by means of non-perception as a logical mark (*anupalabdhi-liṅga*),
because in no case is a contradiction established.
Consequently, since there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the essential reason (*svabhāva-hetu*) is also discarded.
[Objection: But surely that exists.

For instance, the causal complex for a *śiṃśapā* tree is included within the leaves, trunk, and so forth that produce a tree. If that [complex] were to exist apart from the tree, it would thereby transcend its own cause.
In this way, the conventional usage of "tree" is connected with the mere possession of branches and so forth,
while the conventional usage of "śiṃśapā" is connected with its specific qualities.

If it is asked how that [usage of "tree"] could attain its own nature by transcending that [specificity], then in that case, the causal complex for motion is included within the causal complex of the *śiṃśapā*.
Therefore, if motion and so forth were to transcend that [tree], they would themselves transcend their own causes.
Likewise, the conventional usage of "śiṃśapā" is connected with specific features such as branches,
and the conventional usage of "motion" is connected with those specific features.
"How could it reach itself by overstepping that [nature]?"—this is the same [objection].

If it is argued that "the state of motion has as its cause external factors such as impulsion (*nodana*), and does not depend solely on that specific [nature]," then [we reply]: if impulsion and the rest were part of its very nature (*svabhāva*); [then they would be eternal, and the objection remains].
Therefore, they are merely its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*). Or, if they are not of the same nature as it, then they are merely auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
Then,
having encountered them [and] likewise, the *śiṃśapā* tree possesses the very same nature as movement (*calana*).
[The opponent says: "He begins with *va*. And likewise, how is momentariness established?

If it is argued that [the effects] arise as inherent natures (*svabhāva*) precisely through the entry of adventitious auxiliary causes (*āgantuka-sahakārin*), then in that case, the *śiṃśapā* tree would also be produced from the causal complex of a tree (*vṛkṣa-sāmagrī*) alone, simply through the entry of adventitious auxiliary causes.
Thus, there is no distinction whatsoever.
This is so;
however, while those that produce a *śiṃśapā* tree do so by taking up the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of a tree, those that produce motion do not take up that very same complex.

If it is argued that [the cause] is merely corporeal because it is observed as such, this is not so; for even though there are specific causes of *śiṃśapā* trees that produce trembling, they do not transcend those [general causes].
But the specific causes that produce a tree are not necessarily the causes that produce a *śiṃśapā*, because there is no restrictive rule [to that effect].
It is only those specific causes that produce a *śiṃśapā* which are its producers; however, those things that cause trembling are not like that.

If it is argued that these [causes] are merely adventitious auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), then in that case, having obtained those [auxiliaries], some things—even though they possess a similar nature—are capable of producing an effect, whereas those that have not obtained the auxiliaries are not so.
Consequently, there would be no distinction between them, such that one could say "it is this" or "it is like that. (64)
Therefore, there is simply no coexistence of two contradictory things;
and for those that do coexist, there is necessarily a relationship of priority and posteriority.
For things that are not of this nature, such as substance, quality, and action, there is merely the status of being limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

However, there can be no coexistence of those contradictory [qualities], because the individuals are distinct and because the universals have different substrata. And if that is so, how could there be momentariness?
And if one admits a difference in kind (*vaijātya*), how can there even be talk of inference?
If you say, "Let there be no inference," we reply: No—for without that [inference], it could not be established.
For there is no direct perception regarding momentariness,
because there is no such ascertainment;
for the validity of perception applies only to an object that has been apprehended and ascertained.
Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Now, it may be argued that the present moment is the object of direct perception (*adhyakṣagocara*),
and that this [present moment] does not consist of preceding and succeeding moments.
If it is argued that the very ascertainment of presentness is the ascertainment of difference— what is intended by your venerable self in this regard?
If the subject itself, such as blue and so forth [is what is meant], then nothing is untenable.
Because that [property] is common to both stability and instability.
Now, regarding the property (*dharma*): even if there is certainty regarding its distinctions, what has happened to the substratum (*dharmin*)?
For it is distinct from that [property].
If it is argued that it is contradictory for a single entity to be both present and non-present— if that were its being existent and non-existent— that is not so;
for we do not accept that,
since there is recognition [of the entity] precisely as having that same nature.
If it is argued that there can be no connection between the existent and the non-existent—what is so incongruous about it?
For such a connection is possible, just as it is with cognition.

If it is argued that it is impossible for a single entity to have multiple connections sequentially—then at least its existence must be established; however, the distinction is that while the notion of a momentary entity may be erroneous, the notion of [the self] does not even exist.
Let it be that there is neither direct perception nor inference regarding momentariness;
nevertheless, let there be doubt.
If it is argued that the Cārvāka’s desired goal is established even by this much—it is said in reply:
there is no doubt regarding the stability and perception [of objects], nor regarding their validity, because of contradiction; for by what means could there be a certainty of identity in a moment?
Therefore, it is considered stable. //17//
For when that perception [of identity] is stable, doubt does not arise spontaneously;
this is because recognition is difficult to deny.
Nor is there doubt regarding its validity;
For that [doubt] is not universal, because it involves a contradiction.
To explain: if validity is not established, even doubt cannot be established;
or, if it is established, then validity itself must also be established.

(68) Since certainty is dependent upon that [determination], and since the two alternatives are not perceived, what is the meaning of doubt? Furthermore, if those two are seen, how could that [certainty] be entirely unestablished? By this, the claim that the conventional usage of that [doubt] is devoid of any valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇika*) is refuted.
If it is argued that since validity is not established in every respect, that [recognition] is also unestablished—

given that there is doubt regarding validity in the case at hand because of the observation of deviation in instances such as hair that has been cut and grown back again— we say no, because you yourself also accept the certainty of oneness.
Alternatively, if this is not accepted, nothing at all would be established.
If you argue that it may be established where there is an absence of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharma*), then by that very fact, stability (*sthiratva*) is also ascertained.
If you say that this [absence] is what is being doubted here, the same applies to the other case.
If it is argued that there is also some kind of certainty in certain cases, the solution is the same.
Now, if this causality were the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity, like its blueness and so forth, [then it would always be perceived].
In that case, it would be common to all.
For blue is not blue only in relation to someone.
Now, suppose it is adventitious (*aupādhika*).
In that case, if the adjunct (*upādhi*) were also inherent (*svābhāvika*), it would follow that it too possesses that same nature;
if, however, it were adventitious (*aupādhika*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Alternatively, if its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*) were also its very essence;

If it is argued that one should act starting from its arising because a stable entity possesses a single nature, it is said in reply: [Kārikā 1.175] Even blue and other such things do not exist as real entities if they disregard the power of their causes.
Is it not common sense that "that which is capable of producing a certain effect is connected with that [cause] in that regard"? 18.

By demonstrating that the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is conceptual through its difference from blue and so forth—which are common to all—blue and so forth must be accepted as ultimately real (*pāramārthika*);
otherwise, it would be impossible for the causal relationship to be non-ultimate by virtue of being different from them.
Furthermore, if the causal relationship were non-ultimate, blue and so forth could not possibly be ultimately real.
Because it would follow that [the other] is eternal;
therefore, if this were ultimate, the other would likewise be so, or else neither would be.
[Verse 1.176] It is also not tenable to argue: “How could one [cause] produce multiple, mutually contradictory effects?

If you say it is because that is its very nature (*tatsvabhāvatvāt*), then it should produce them from the very moment of its arising, since there is no difference [in its nature]. This too is incorrect.

Because its nature is established as performing various effects when accompanied by their respective auxiliary conditions (or because its conventional designation as having such a nature is established),
and this is indeed common to all, since it is perceived as such by everyone.
For there is no commonality other than that of blue and so forth.
This might be argued:
let it be stable.
Nevertheless, causality is not possible for that which is eternal and omnipresent.
For instance, causality is determined through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka),
not by positive concomitance alone.
Because this would lead to an over-extension [of the argument],

and because it is impossible for eternal and omnipresent entities to possess negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Nor is it correct to say that such concomitance exists precisely because it is qualified by limiting conditions (*upādhi*).
Because even when connected with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that which has become such [the Self] lacks agency;
for what is produced by that [adjunct] would either be non-eternal or eternal for it.
It cannot be the first case, as before.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
for the same reason as before; moreover, even in that case, the exclusion (vyatireka) would be merely a limiting adjunct (upādhi).
Not [is it] his; because there is no distinction. If it is argued that [it belongs] to one who possesses that—[it is not so;
because there is no distinction]. If it is argued that [it belongs] to one who possesses that—[it is not so; because there is no distinction].
No; for there exists no entity other than that [entity] and its limiting adjunct (upādhi),
or, if such an entity did exist, it would itself be the cause.

To this it is replied: [Kārikā 1.178] "For causality is indeed the state of prior existence, which is measured by whatever means possible; otherwise, there could be no cognition of the subject (dharmin), even in the case of an all-pervading eternal entity. (19)

It would indeed be so, if causality consisted solely of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka); however, [causality] is rather the necessary prior existence of the cause relative to the effect.

And that [causal relation] is determined in some cases through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), and in others through the means of valid cognition that apprehends the locus (dharmin).
Otherwise, the inference of a cause from an effect would never occur anywhere.
Because its conformity to that [cause] is not perceived, or because if it were perceived, there would be no room for an effect as a logical mark (*kāryaliṅga*);
for that [cause] is established through direct perception alone. Furthermore, the establishment [of a cause] elsewhere is not prevented by the observation of conformity to things of that same class.

[Ku. 1.179] Even so, it might be argued that a cause is established from its effect only when the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) follows the internal logic of the case, because such is observed elsewhere. If this is said, we reply: no—because the rule must be restricted due to sublation (bādha), and because there is no pervasion (avyāpti) since there is no subverting argument (bādhaka) against the contrary case.
And because there is equality in superiority merely by being perceived;
furthermore, this will be explained in detail regarding Īśvara.

If it is argued that the subverting proof (*bādhaka*) is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all-pervading things would be causes with respect to everything simply by virtue of their mere positive concomitance (*anvaya-mātra-viśeṣa*), we say no—because [the cause] possesses a specific nature characterized by both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-vaj-jātīyatayā*), and because there is a subverting proof against such a [universal] case.
Because it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

For instance, since an effect is observed to possess an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), even that which has an unobserved substratum must likewise have a cause of that same class. In the absence of a substratum, what could serve as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) by virtue of its proximity?
And in the absence of that, how could even an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) provide any assistance?

Furthermore, there would either be no production at all, or production would occur constantly, or production would occur everywhere. Even so, since the production occurs in a specific location solely due to the efficacy of the efficient cause (*nimitta*), that very location must necessarily be depended upon.

Thus, once a location is established in general, who could prevent the establishment of something distinct from earth and the other elements, given the exclusion of those others? The same logic should be applied to the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyinimitta*).

[1.180] Thus, this peerless power of co-operation— called *māyā* because it is difficult to fathom, *prakṛti* because it is the root, and *avidyā* because of its fear-inducing nature regarding awakening— may that Lord, in whom the tumultuous waves of the fabrication of the phenomenal world have ceased, being peaceful, bestow his delight upon my mind as its direct witness.
Thus ends the first chapter in the glorious *Nyāyakusumāñjali*.
